intro: Olga Gurevich’s recording was released through Musopen’s Set Chopin Free project. Compare the broad middle with the running outer music; her complete access file lasts about 1:47.
question: How much space does Gurevich give the middle of the waltz?

cues.title: One release, one pianist
cues.text: This is Gurevich’s performance from Musopen’s Set Chopin Free project, not a historical disc transfer. Follow the rapid upper line while keeping the separate three-beat accompaniment in mind.
cues.evidence: Commons identifies Olga Gurevich and the Set Chopin Free recording release. The opening report records 7–8.6 detected attacks per second; the listening invitation does not identify individual beats.

cues.title: A less crowded surface
cues.text: The middle leaves more room between attacks and initially withdraws in recorded weight. Compare how the longer melodic gestures sit above the continuing accompaniment.
cues.evidence: A 0:34 novelty boundary precedes the 0:35 window at −19.3 dB and 3.2 attacks per second, against 6–8 in the preceding stretch.

cues.title: A strong renewed start
cues.text: The return of denser activity begins with the strongest measured five-second window in this performance. Listen for how that renewed weight changes the running line without changing its identity.
cues.evidence: The 1:04 boundary leads to the loudest relative-level window at 1:05, −7.8 dB and 8.6 detected attacks per second. This is a within-recording measurement only.

cues.title: Allowing the ending to fade
cues.text: The closing phrase leaves a short final decay rather than a long silent extension. Use the disappearance of the piano sound, not only the end of the file, when comparing the three endings.
cues.evidence: The report retains sound at 1:40, then reaches −56.3 dB with no detected attacks at 1:45; file duration is 107.4 seconds.

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
